KEY MESSAGE 1... 
Following the theme of summer and now early Meteorological Fall
of 2026, yet another severe weather event is expected across NE
Ohio and NW PA this afternoon and evening. Afternoon visible
satellite and water vapor loops show a strong mid/upper
shortwave trough progressing from the Upper Midwest into the
Great Lakes. This is eroding the northern periphery of an
unseasonably strong mid/upper ridge centered over the SE CONUS.
The surface low associated with the mid/upper shortwave is near
Hudson Bay and will progress east into northern Quebec tonight,
dragging a cold front across our region. Despite the surface low
being displaced so far north, plenty of jet dynamics will
accompany the mid/upper shortwave this evening to enhance height
falls and large scale ascent as well as to increase deep layer
shear. This forcing coupled with moderate instability (MLCAPE of
1000-1500 J/Kg) will support a healthy line of convection.

In terms of timing and details, dying convection from last night
has left a band of showers over Lower Michigan, Indiana, and
extreme NW Ohio early this afternoon. This is setting up a
differential heating boundary/pre-frontal trough over NW Ohio,
which will act as the main trigger to ignite the main line of
convection this evening as the shortwave and associated forcing
overspread the area. Out ahead of this pre-frontal trough, a
lake breeze boundary may set up east of Cleveland this
afternoon. Forecast soundings do not have much of a cap to erode
since mid-level lapse rates are weak ( 5 to 5.5 C/Km) and the
atmosphere is quite warm through the entire boundary layer, so
expect initial scattered convection to develop between 18 and
20Z along the lake breeze and impact NE Ohio and NW PA. A few of
these storms could produce damaging winds since strong surface
heating has created steep low-level lapse rates and resultant
high DCAPE over 800 J/Kg. However, the main show will be with
the line of convection that develops on the pre-frontal trough
this evening. Consensus among HREF CAMS and the RRFS is for this
line to develop from roughly the Lake Erie Islands to Marion
after 20 or 21Z then propagate east through the Cleveland and
Akron areas around 23Z and through NW PA by 01Z. The
aforementioned instability coupled with deep layer effective
shear increasing to 40-50 knots will support bowing segments
capable of damaging winds. Any bowing segments will also need to
be watched for isolated QLCS tornadoes since 0-3 Km shear will
be over 30 knots and will try to orient normal to the line at
times. Surface to 1 Km shear of 20-25 knots also supports the
isolated tornado threat. Finally, storm cell movement will be
fast (generally over 40 knots to the E and SE), but any repeated
rounds of convection could result in locally excessive rainfall
and flash flooding since PWATS are running unseasonably high 
(1.7 to 2 inches) and soundings show a deep warm cloud layer. 
This will mainly occur if parts of NE Ohio and NW PA see heavy 
rain from the initial scattered convection late this afternoon 
before the main line crosses the region this evening.

KEY MESSAGE 2... 
There will be a break in the rain showers most of tonight behind
the line of convection, but a second mid/upper shortwave will
progress across the Great Lakes and Upper Ohio Valley Thursday.
The right entrance region of the mid/upper jet will lead to a
weak surface wave that will ride along the front, causing the
frontal boundary to briefly stall over northern or central Ohio
Thursday morning. This wave and right entrance ascent should
generate additional showers north of the boundary Thursday
morning into the afternoon, especially along and south of I-80 
and I-76. CAMS are in agreement with this, so increase POPS from
12 to 18Z. The front will finally push south behind this wave 
late Thursday afternoon and Thursday night allowing a large 
Canadian high at the surface to build down across the Great 
Lakes. This will bring dry and cooler, much more seasonable 
weather for Thursday night and Friday. 

KEY MESSAGE 3...
Unfortunately, the more typical mid September weather will not 
last long as a warm, humid, and unsettled pattern looks to 
quickly return this weekend. A couple of mid/upper troughs and
associated closed lows progressing into the Pacific Northwest
between Saturday and Wednesday will build an elongated mid/upper
ridge across the south central and SE CONUS. This will allow
temperatures well into the 80s and dew points in the upper 60s 
to around 70 to build back into the region Saturday and largely 
remain through Wednesday. Active quasi-zonal mid/upper flow 
across the Great Lakes on the northern periphery of the 
elongated ridge will send shortwave energy near or north of the 
region at times interacting with a wavering frontal boundary,
